Notes: Year Established basis: Y. Alexandre, 'The Settlement History of Nazareth in the Iron Age and Early Roman Period', 'Atiqot 98 (IAA), excavation beside the Franciscan Church of the Annunciation: Stratum II, 'from the late Hellenistic to the Early Roman period' (late 2nd c. BCE to first third of 2nd c. CE; late 2nd c. BCE = -125, c.). The dwelling had a three-level complex of subterranean pits/silos with discarded potsherds 'perhaps attesting to the Jewish practice of ritual defilement'; 'similar findings were documented at other Jewish villages of the Early Roman period in Galilee'. Earliest documented Jewish village at the site; start coincides with the Hasmonean takeover of Galilee. An earlier Iron IIA-B stratum (10th-early 8th c. BCE) exists but is not identified as Israelite in the sources consulted, so it is not used for Year Established. Presence of a small Jewish village; no count.

K. Dark (Univ. of Reading, Bible and Interpretation, July 2020): 'Nazareth was inhabited from at least the early first century, and probably the Late Hellenistic period onward.' Probable Late Hellenistic (Hasmonean-era) beginning of the settlement; Hasmonean period midpoint -90 used (c.). Presence; no count.

Luke 1:5 and 1:26-27: 'In the days of King Herod of Judea' the angel Gabriel was sent 'to a town in Galilee called Nazareth' to Mary, engaged to Joseph of the house of David; Luke 2:39: 'they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth'. Literary (Gospel) attestation of a Jewish family resident in Nazareth before Herod's death (4 BCE); c. 5 BCE. Historicity of the infancy narratives is debated. Presence of named individuals; no count.

K. Dark (2020): limestone vessel fragments 'of the type characteristic of the Early Roman-period Jewish communities in Galilee' from three sites (incl. Sisters of Nazareth Convent and Church of the Annunciation); pottery at the Annunciation site from the early 1st to the 4th c.; the combined evidence shows Nazareth inhabited 'from at least the early first century' as an agricultural Jewish community. Early 1st c. CE, c. 15 used. Presence; no count.

C. A. Evans, Jesus and His World: The Archaeological Evidence (2012), ch. 1: 'Nazareth was a small village with a population somewhere between 200 and 400' at the time of Jesus; 'In all likelihood not a single non-Jew lived in Nazareth at this time'; 'The first-century village of Nazareth probably occupied no more than four hectares.' Range 200-400, midpoint 300. Total population of an entirely Jewish village per the source. Year: time of Jesus, early 1st c. CE (c. 15). Method not stated (based on small built-up area and modest dwellings).

J. D. Crossan and J. L. Reed, Excavating Jesus (2001), as summarised by G. K. Barr, 'Jesus in Nazareth', Irish Biblical Studies 26/2 (2005): Crossan and Reed portray Nazareth as 'absolutely insignificant and entirely Jewish'; 'A population of two to four hundred is assumed, all being poor peasants.' Range 200-400, midpoint 300. Total population of an entirely Jewish village per the source. Year: time of Jesus (c. 15). Barr notes Crossan and Reed record that a priestly family resettled in Nazareth after 135 CE (outside period). Original book not checked.

J. F. Strange (E. Meyers and J. Strange, Archaeology, the Rabbis, and Early Christianity, 1981) originally calculated the population of Nazareth at the time of Christ as 'roughly 1,600 to 2,000 people' (midpoint 1800), as reported by Wikipedia, which also states Nazareth was 'a strongly Jewish settlement in the Roman period' (citing Finegan 1992) and 'a Jewish village during the Roman and Byzantine periods'. Total population of a Jewish village per the source. Later revised by Strange himself (next row). Original not checked; time of Jesus, c. 15. [Review fix: Population 1800 moved to Notes; Strange himself revised this 1981 figure to a maximum of about 480 (separate row)]

J. F. Strange, 'Nazareth', Anchor Bible Dictionary (1992), revised his earlier estimate down to 'a maximum of about 480' inhabitants at the time of Christ, as reported by Wikipedia (which describes Roman-period Nazareth as a strongly Jewish settlement). Upper bound, used as given. Total population of a Jewish village per the source. Original not checked; time of Jesus, c. 15. The same page also cites S. Korb (2010) for 'a population of 400 and one public bath' (popular book; not given its own row).

K. Dark's Nazareth Archaeological Project (Routledge 2020), as reported by D. Keys (The Independent) and quoted in this blog post (D. Armstrong, 2023): Nazareth 'probably had a population of up to 1,000' rather than 'a small-to-medium sized village of 100-500, as previously thought'. Population left blank: this page does not itself state that the town was Jewish (Dark elsewhere describes it as a Jewish community), and the figure is an upper bound reported second-hand. Same page: mid-1st-c. anti-Roman rebels dug underground hiding places 'big enough to shelter at least 100 people' (a capacity, not a population).

Luke 4:16: 'When he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, as was his custom'; 4:28-29: 'all in the synagogue were filled with rage' and drove him out of 'the town'. Literary attestation of a Jewish congregation (synagogue gathering) in Nazareth during Jesus' ministry, c. 30 CE. No synagogue building has been found archaeologically. Presence of an organised Jewish community; no count.

Israel Antiquities Authority (Dec. 2009; excavation director Yardenna Alexandre), next to the Church of the Annunciation: first excavated dwelling of Early Roman Nazareth (1st-2nd c. CE), 'small and modest' and 'most likely typical of the dwellings in Nazareth in that period'; 'several fragments of chalk vessels were found, which were only used by Jews in this period'. IAA: 'in the first century CE Nazareth was a small Jewish village'. 1st c. CE midpoint 50 (c.). Presence of a small Jewish village; no count.

Sisters of Nazareth Convent (K. Dark, Nazareth Archaeological Project from 2006): 'a first-century courtyard house that was partially hewn from naturally occurring rock', with tombs and a cistern on the site; Dark concludes Nazareth 'was particularly Jewish in its identity', unlike Sepphoris. 1st c. CE midpoint 50 (c.). Presence; no count.

IAA 2009 excavation (Y. Alexandre): a hewn pit 'whose entrance was apparently camouflaged' was 'probably hewn as part of the preparations by the Jews to protect themselves during the Great Revolt against the Romans in 67 CE'. Event: Jewish residents prepared hiding places in the First Revolt. No count.

K. Dark (2020): storage pits in central Nazareth were reused as refuges during the First Revolt, with 'narrow burrow-like tunnels characteristic of hiding places from the period of the Jewish Revolts'. Event: Jewish residents' preparations against the Romans, c. 66-67 CE. No evidence found of destruction or abandonment of the village in 67-70. No count.
